messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 69-year-old Vietnamese American man who works as a nanny, a role he took on after his wife died, to stay connected to the energy of young children. Two years ago, while caring for three-year-old Leo, the son of a neighbor, Minh watched the boy suddenly seize during a high fever. He called 911, but in the minutes before the ambulance arrived he could do nothing but hold Leo as the child’s body stiffened and his eyes rolled back. The diagnosis was bacterial meningitis; Leo survived after weeks in the ICU. Minh stopped telling the story after a few attempts because he could never get the sequence straight—the timeline felt scrambled, the details shifting—and the few times he tried, the memory would flood him with such sensory force that his hands would tremble and his chest would tighten as if he were back in that living room. He had come to believe that the person he was before that afternoon no longer existed; the man who had felt competent and calm with children had been replaced by someone who startled at a child’s cough and who saw hidden threats in ordinary faces. That sense of being permanently damaged, of having crossed a line he could not uncross, made the memory feel less like a recollection and more like a trap he was still living inside. Through the months that followed, Minh developed a private rhythm of survival. He tried hard not to think about Leo’s seizure or the hospital, but the more he pushed the memory away, the more it erupted with vivid, present-tense clarity—the smell of Leo’s skin, the pitch of his mother’s scream, the blue of the paramedic’s gloves. He kept his mind occupied constantly: crossword puzzles, long bus rides, cooking elaborate meals he barely ate. And he began to avoid medical settings altogether. When Leo’s mother asked Minh to accompany them to a follow-up pediatric appointment, he invented a stomachache and stayed home. He stopped getting his own blood pressure checked, telling himself the numbers would only confirm what he already knew: that something inside him had broken irreparably. Minh’s distrust of others grew quietly but steadily; he noticed the way people’s eyes slid away when he spoke about the event, and he became certain they were hiding their judgment of his failure. This distrust reinforced the memory’s power—if he could not trust others to tell him the truth, then the only reality he could rely on was the one that played in his mind, and that reality insisted the event was still happening. In turn, the intrusive, present-tense memory confirmed his belief that he had permanently changed: how could he be the same person if his past felt more alive than his present? He found himself unable to form a coherent narrative of what had happened, not just to the emergency room staff right after, but even to himself alone at night. The fragments would not arrange themselves into a story with a beginning, middle, and end; they stayed as isolated, unbearable moments. Suppressing those moments only made them sharper, and the cycle tightened. At work, Minh now avoids taking care of any child who shows the slightest sign of illness, even a sniffle, and he has begun turning down families with toddlers, the age Leo was. He tells his supervisor he is tired, but the truth is that a feverish child triggers a cascade of vivid, physical memory that leaves him drenched in sweat and unable to speak. His avoidance of medical care almost cost him his own health when he ignored chest pains for three weeks, attributing them to age rather than the panic his body was holding. What finally brought Minh to a therapist was a moment three weeks ago: he was pushing a stroller through the park and a toddler on a blanket coughed—a small, ordinary sound—and Minh’s vision went gray. He dropped to his knees, convinced Leo was seizing again, and did not recognize the child’s mother trying to help him up. He came home that evening and sat in the dark, unable to name who he had become. He is terrified that he will never be able to hold a crying child again without collapsing inside, but he is more frightened that if he does not change course, the man he used to be will vanish entirely, leaving only this trembling stranger in his place.
